title: Dual-Functional Substrate-Integrated Accelerometer-Tactile Architecture for Absolute and Differential Motion Artifact Monitoring and Dual-Modality Arterial Pulse Measurement: Part II—Experimental Investigation
content: Background: A two-degree-of-freedom (2-DOF) formulation of the tissue-contact-sensor (TCS) stack in a substrate-integrated accelerometer (ACC)-tactile architecture provides a theoretical basis for complementary sensing of motion artifacts (MA), quantified as baseline drift (BD), and arterial pulse motion. Aim: This second of two parts experimentally investigates predicted relationships between tactile sensor and ACC outputs at the carotid artery (CA) and radial artery (RA) and complementary sensing characteristics. Methods: Using a micro/nano-fabricated tactile sensor integrated with a three-axis ACC attached to its substrate, arterial pulse signals were measured at the CA and RA in healthy subjects. A single-degree-of-freedom time-frequency (SDOF-TF) method analyzed tactile sensor and ACC outputs for BD, harmonic amplitudes, instantaneous frequency (IF), instantaneous initial phase (IIP), heart rate (HR), heart rate variability (HRV), respiration rate (RR), and respiration modulation (RM). Results: The tactile sensor provided cleaner arterial pulse signals than the z-axis ACC output and was relatively robust to MA. The absolute harmonic amplitudes of the ACC output were larger than those of the tactile sensor, consistent with the 2-DOF model, whereas normalized harmonic distributions relative to the first harmonic did not quantitatively reproduce the predicted frequency-dependent relationship, indicating measurement errors in the ACC output. Three-axis ACC measurements revealed radial, lateral, and axial components of arterial wall motion and MA. HR and RR were relatively consistent between outputs, whereas larger differences occurred in HRV and RM. Significance: This ACC-tactile architecture provides a framework for preliminary identification of relative relationships among TCS system parameters from complementary tactile and ACC measurements. The validated relative parameter relationships, together with the robustness of time-based indices to MA in the tactile output, provide a basis for deeper exploration of the model and tactile and ACC outputs for quantitative TCS parameter identification and TCS–artery interaction characterization at both arterial sites.
